title: eBay pays $46M to journalists it targeted in bizarre harassment campaign
title_zh: eBay 向其在离奇骚扰活动中针对的记者支付 4600 万美元

eBay and three former executives agreed to pay nearly $56 million in a settlement over a macabre campaign of cyberstalking and harassment that targeted two journalists in 2019.
As we’ve previously written , the case involved deliveries of live cockroaches, a funeral wreath, a book about surviving the loss of a spouse, and a bloody pig mask to the home of a couple who run a news website. There were also harassing messages sent via email and Twitter, and an attempt to install a GPS tracking device on the victims’ car. Criminal charges resulted in guilty pleas and prison terms for former eBay employees.
The victims were Ina and David Steiner of Natick, Massachusetts, who run the news website EcommerceBytes. “David and I officially settled the lawsuit we filed in 2021 against eBay and its former executives over the stalking and harassment campaign we endured in 2019 designed to stop our reporting,” Ina Steiner wrote on EcommerceBytes yesterday. “The landmark civil rights settlement includes $55.7 million in compensation and charitable commitments.”
eBay will pay $46.15 million in compensation to the Steiners, announced Scalli Murphy Law, the Steiners’ law firm. The settlement includes another $2 million in compensation from former eBay CEO Devin Wenig, $500,000 from former eBay Senior Vice President of Global Operations Wendy Jones, and $50,000 from former eBay Chief Communications Officer Steve Wymer.
eBay will give $6 million to various charities, while “Wenig will contribute an additional $1 million to a charity dedicated to protecting First Amendment rights in the name of Ina Steiner,” the announcement said. The law firm said that additional “settlements were reached with all other eBay employees named in the civil action.” eBay reported $3.1 billion in revenue and $512 million in net income in its most recent quarterly report.
Other former execs went to prison
The main settlement with eBay and former executives did not have any confidentiality restrictions, and it required eBay to “issue a strongly-worded public statement regarding the conduct” of the executives “and the culture of the company in 2019,” the Steiners’ law firm said.
eBay issued that statement today, saying that “what the Steiners were subjected to by former eBay employees in 2019 was wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened. We condemn, in the strongest terms possible, the employees who perpetrated and pled guilty to criminal charges for the misconduct against Ina and David Steiner. We also acknowledge the unprofessional tone in internal communications demonstrated, to different degrees and number, by Mr. Wenig, Mr. Wymer, and Ms. Jones.”
eBay said that since the 2019 events, “new leaders have joined the company and eBay has strengthened its policies, procedures, controls and training consistent with the company’s ongoing commitment to uphold high standards of conduct and ethics.”
Seven former eBay employees and contractors pleaded guilty , and prison sentences were issued to former eBay security executives James Baugh (57 months), David Harville (24 months), Philip Cooke (18 months), and Stephanie Popp (12 months). Two others received a year in home confinement and another was sentenced to time served and a year of supervised release.
“I want to see ashes… Whatever it takes”
Wenig and Wymer were not charged criminally but were accused in the civil lawsuit of giving employees “carte blanche authority” to carry out the harassment campaign.
“Defendants Wenig and Wymer provided the other Defendants with carte blanche authority to terminate the reporting of the Steiners by whatever means necessary, with Defendant Wymer expressing ‘…I want to see ashes. As long as it takes. Whatever it takes.’ Defendant Wymer promised the Defendants he would, ’embrace managing any bad fallout’ if the plan went south, further directing, ‘We need to STOP her,’” the lawsuit filed in 2021 said.
The harassment was allegedly spurred in part by an April 2019 article titled, “eBay CEO Devin Wenig Earns 152 Times That of Employees.” An FBI affidavit included messages exchanged between Wenig and Wymer about that article and other coverage of eBay by EcommerceBytes. Wenig, identified in the affidavit as “Executive 1,” told Wymer to “take her down” in reference to Ina Steiner.
Wenig provided a statement today saying the “harassment was deliberately done in secret and without my knowledge,” and that he is “pleased that a meaningful portion of my settlement will go directly to a non-profit committed to protecting freedom of the press.” eBay said in 2020 that its “internal investigation found that, while Mr. Wenig’s communications were inappropriate, there was no evidence that he knew in advance about or authorized the actions that were later directed toward the blogger and her husband.”
An amended complaint filed in 2023 described Jones’ alleged role: “Defendant Jones asked Defendant Baugh if he could find a way to deal with the issue ‘off the radar since comms and legal couldn’t handle it.’ Jones added, ‘Just get it done. I don’t want to know the details, just make sure you sync with Wymer.’ After the lunch meeting, Defendant Baugh provided regular updates to Defendant Jones.”
eBay itself faced criminal charges and agreed to pay a $3 million fine in 2024, while entering into a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice.
As a result of the settlement, the Steiners yesterday submitted a court filing to withdraw their complaint and end the civil lawsuit.
“Our clients wanted to uncover the truth, protect journalists and publishers, hold those responsible accountable, deter future corporate misconduct, and help ensure others would never have to endure what they experienced,” lawyer Christopher Murphy said. “Through years of discovery, motion [filing], and trial preparation, we were able to accomplish those objectives while securing meaningful compensation for two wonderful people.”
This article was updated with additional details about Devin Wenig and a statement from Wenig.
